Photons are splatted using a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel, storing them as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light [S1].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S1]. The source explicitly states that photons are splatted using a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel, and that they are stored as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light.

Voxels are repeated for adjacent bricks for fast hardware-supported filtering, but copying photons directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to many thread collisions and bandwidth issues [S1].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S1]. The passage explicitly states: 'We mentioned in Sec. 4 that this redundancy is necessary for fast hardware-supported filtering. While thread collisions are rare for the initial splat, we found that copying the photon directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to many collisions that affect performance significantly. This parallel random scattering, further, results in bandwidth issues.' This matches the claim's assertion that voxels are repeated for fast hardware-supported filtering and that copying photons directly to adjacent bricks causes thread collisions and bandwidth issues.

Atomic add operations are used to handle multiple photons ending up in the same voxel, though they are currently only available for integer textures, requiring a 16-bit normalized texture format denormalized upon access [S1].

The claim states that atomic add operations are used to handle multiple photons in the same voxel, which is supported by the text: 'Because several photons might end up in the same voxel, we need to rely on an atomic add.' The claim also states these operations are currently only available for integer textures, supported by: 'atomic add operations are currently only available for integer textures.' Finally, the claim mentions using a 16-bit normalized texture format denormalized upon access, supported by: 'We can easily address this issue by using a 16bit normalized texture format, that is denormalized when accessing the value later.'
